item.title: Who Is Planting Backdoors in Ledger Crypto Wallets? (122 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.zetter-zeroday.com/who-is-planting-backdoors-in-ledger-crypto-wallets/, See on Hacker News

After crypto wallet maker Ledger announced Friday that a backdoor embedded in a handful of Ledger wallets sold in SouthEast Asia allowed thieves to hijack around $102 million in crypto from their owners, news has emerged of other Ledger wallets sold in Germany also having implants.

The hardware implants were originally found on an unknown number of Ledger Nano X wallets sold by an authorized Ledger reseller called CryptoBilis based in Malaysia. Ledger said the implants were found on a limited number of devices, all sold by the same seller. But a Ledger device owner in Europe has since said that he found an implant on a Nano X that he purchased at a large European electronics chain store in August and a second one he purchased this weekend at another store in the same chain. He believes these indicate that Ledger’s supply-chain has been compromised.

Since then, users and researchers have also reported finding implants in Ledger Flex and Ledger Stax devices – two of Ledger's more recent line of devices used for securely storing keys used to access a device owner's crypto accounts.

The implants are not the first to be found on Ledger wallets. Famed hardware hacker Joe Grand found implants on several Nano X wallets earlier this year and notified Ledger about them in March, raising questions about Ledger's urgency in addressing the issue. Many of the implants discovered more recently appear to be more sophisticated iterations of the ones that Grand found.

The implants Grand discovered were also all in wallets sold by unauthorized online sellers who seemingly ran fly-by-night operations that weren’t in business for long. But the implants found in wallets sold by CryptoBilis and the European electronics chain indicate the attackers have switched tactics and may be deliberately compromising wallets sold by authorized resellers now. Ledger and its competitor Trezor have cautioned users for years to buy wallets only from their web sites or from authorized resellers. But the recent compromises indicate that attackers are deliberately targeting authorized sellers to exploit customer trust in them and to get wider distribution for implanted devices. What’s more, the attackers have become more skilled and systematic in their method for compromising the wallets, making it more difficult to detect the implants, Grand and other researchers say.

It's not clear how long the implants have been sitting in the sold devices, but last week a coordinated heist resulted in millions of dollars in crypto being stolen from the device and accountholders. According to blockchain research company Bitquery, crypto was stolen from about 315 accounts connected to compromised CryptoBilis Ledger devices alone, and is currently valued at around $102 million. The stolen funds include Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron and other cryptocurrencies. Some of the funds have reportedly been frozen in the accounts to which the thieves transferred it, and other funds appear to be in accounts that have been flagged for fraud. And it's not clear if funds were also stolen from Ledger owners who purchased their devices from other sellers.

Ledger, based in France, wrote in statement posted to X that it had asked CryptoBilis to halt all sales and shipments of Ledger devices until it could conduct an investigation. CryptoBilis — which is authorized to sell Ledger wallets in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines — wrote on its web site that it is cooperating with Ledger’s investigation.

But a user going by the name Johannes wrote on X over the weekend that he had purchased a Ledger Nano X wallet in person from a MediaMarkt store that had an implant. MediaMarkt is Germany’s equivalent to BestBuy and has 1,000 stores in ten European countries. It’s listed as an authorized reseller of Ledger wallets in Austria, Germany, Spain and Turkey.

Johannes told Zero Day he purchased the wallet in August in a MediaMarkt store in Germany but only took the device apart this weekend following reports that implants had been found. He posted photos of an antenna and implant in his device. Johannes said that he has had no crypto stolen.

In an update to X this weekend, Ledger suggested the implant problem may stem from authorized resellers obtaining Ledger wallets from illegitimate sources or reselling wallets that were bought and returned to them — after being compromised.

“We are reminding our authorized resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products,” Ledger wrote. “This is an ongoing threat that doesn’t just impact Ledger, but the whole ecosystem, and we are calling others in the space to work with us on making improvements for users…. Raising the bar on physical supply-chain integrity benefits the entire ecosystem.”

But Johannes, who purchased a second Ledger wallet from another MediaMarkt store on Monday and found an implant in it as well thinks this suggests that Ledger’s supply chain has been compromised.

“This indicates a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe,” he wrote on X. He says he initially thought his two compromised devices might have been return items that the store then resold as new, but a MediaMarkt employee told him they were new devices and that returns are sent back to Ledger, not re-sold.

Ledger did not respond to an inquiry from Zero Day, but the company wrote on X that there is currently "no indication that Ledger's security infrastructure, systems or services have been compromised.

The issue raises questions about Ledger’s response to the implants and its transparency to customers. After Grand notified the company last March about implants he found in Ledger wallets, the company told him it would investigate to determine who was behind the implants. But Grand says he never received any followup until months later when he asked about it, and someone at Ledger told him they had found no evidence that someone had used the implants to steal crypto from device owners.

But the situation began to change after this.

If you find this article valuable, you can leave a one-time tip to express appreciation to the author.

In April and May, Grand published his implant findings online and gave two presentations about them at conferences in April and May. Mark Karpelès, a French businessman and former CEO of the infamous bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox who was charged with fraud following the collapse of his business, saw Grand's research online and decided to purchase Ledger wallets to see if he could find implants in them as well. He obtained two wallets and found more advanced iterations of the implant Grand discovered and published his findings online last month.

Karpelès's notoriety in the crypto world caused information about the implants to spread widely in the crypto community, which may be why the heists occurred last week. The attackers may have been waiting until they had amassed many wallets with large balances associated with them before pulling off a widespread heist of funds. But once news about the implants began to spread, this may have spurred the thieves to quickly grab as much crypto as they could from wallets already compromised, before wallet owners could move to protect those funds. Some people online have been praising Karpelès for exposing the implants and an operation that might have gone unnoticed for years until he wrote about it.

Evolving Backdoors

Grand began looking at Ledger wallets in August 2025 after someone published a Reddit post indicating he had found something in his Ledger Nano X wallet. The owner, who purchased the wallet from an online marketplace in Thailand, cracked opened the wallet’s casing and found extra circuitry that should not have been there. He sent the wallet to Grand to see if he could confirm it was a backdoor and determine what it was designed to do.

Inside the device, Grand found an extra board as well as an antenna, LTE module and eSIM. He determined that the implant was stealing the recovery seeds of infected wallets and transmitting them to the attackers. The implant would sit silently on the device until the owner initialized it and caused it to generate a random seed phrase – essentially a password stored on the Ledger device to allow the device holder to access their crypto account. As the device sent each character of the seed phrase to the device's small screen to display to the owner, the implant copied them and stored the data before subsequently using the LTE module, antenna and eSIM to connect to a nearby cell tower and transmit the seed to the hackers.

Grand, who runs Grand Idea Studio, was thrilled with the finding because although there have long been rumors and theoretical claims about hardware implants on wallets he had never seen one in the wild. He purchased eight more Ledger wallets from several online sellers in Thailand and found that four of them were compromised with similar implants. All of the ones Grand purchased came from "sketchy" sellers on Lazada, an e-commerce platform in SouthEast Asia that is a subsidiary of the Chinese company Alibaba Group. The devices were shipped from Thailand.

On March 4, Grand reported his findings to Ledger and had a Zoom call with a team there, and subsequently gave two talks about the backdoors at the Tropicon conference in April and at the Hardwear.IO conference in May and posted his slides online. He also continued to have some e-mail conversations with Ledger before moving to a Signal group chat with some technical staff there as well as with a researcher based in Japan who had purchased some wallets through online sellers there in March and found implants in them.

In September, Karpelès saw Grand’s research and obtained two Ledger wallets, including one purchased at half price from a Chinese seller on Amazon that arrived in a “flawless” shrink-wrapped box from Malaysia. He found implants inside both wallets and published his findings last month on the web site for Tibane Labs, which Karpelès owns and uses to conduct blockchain research and produce open-source tools. The implants operated similar to the ones Grand had found, but they were much more sophisticated in their design and more cleverly hidden to make them harder to spot inside a device.

Karpelès said the version Grand found appeared to be a prototype that had evolved over time. That first-generation involved a bundle of hand-soldered wires that stood out to anyone who opened the devices. The wires connected the implant to the Nano’s screen to grab each character of the randomly-generated seed as they were displayed on the screen.

The more advanced implant used an orange-colored, transparent, custom-built flexible circuit laid over the wallet’s original board and laminated flat onto it and soldered in select places, eliminating the need to solder wires that could be easily seen. To make room for the additional circuit, the hackers had replaced the original battery with a smaller one. Based on some markings, the implant appeared to have been assembled in December 2025 or later.

The second implant, which he found in the device shipped from Malaysia, was the most advanced. Inside the wallet, there appeared to be nothing to distinguish it from an unmodified Nano X device. But a thin black antenna running along the top edge of the board was a giveaway. But every other giveaway from the previous design had been eliminated. The orange flex circuit had been coated with the same black color as the legitimate Ledger board, allowing it to blend in with that component. Part numbers were scraped off, and the original battery was still there. The attackers had simply removed some padding that normally sat behind the screen to make room for the implant. Notably, the attackers had silk-screened a parts number — AC-A2016-NANO-V1.1 — onto the antenna, suggesting it was a custom-built component that had been manufactured to hijack Nano wallets at scale.

“‘NANO' names the target,” Karpelès wrote, “and ‘V1.1’ says it has already been through at least one revision. Someone designed and ordered RF parts for this one device. That is a production run, not a one-off.”

This third-generation version of the implant was “not a hobbyist’s build,” he wrote. “A flex PCB keyed to the Ledger’s own parts, a custom antenna already at its second revision, colour-matched coating and scraped markings all point to planning, a real budget, and a goal of mass production.”

On October 8, the day before the crypto heists went public, Karpelès began posting a series of messages on X about his findings and responding to questions about the implants he found. This is when news of the implants began to spread. The next day, news of the crypto heists emerged, raising questions about whether the attention Karpelès brought to the implants caused the attackers to launch their crypto heister sooner than they had originally planned.

Who Is Behind the Compromised Wallets?

Over the weekend, questions have arisen online about the founders of CryptoBilis and the fact that the company quietly switched owners in March — an acquisition that was not publicly disclosed until this weekend when users on X began pointing fingers at the founders and suggesting they might be behind the compromised devices or at least cooperating with the crypto thieves who stole money from the owners of compromised Ledger devices.

CryptoBilis co-founder Arravind Prabu rejected the accusations and revealed that his company had been acquired by someone else earlier this year and that he and his cofounder had “fully stepped down from all operations, system access, and management” in March. When asked why the acquisition was never made public, Prabu claimed in a lengthy statement that the deal was under an NDA until mid-October, which only enhanced suspicions.

“Since the completion of the handover, we have held zero access, credentials, visibility, or administrative control over CryptoBilis backend systems, customer databases, order histories, or corporate communication channels,” Prabu and his cofounder wrote in their statement. “Under the formal acquisition agreements, all parties were contractually bound to hold off on issuing a joint public announcement until mid-October 2026.”

He says that all suppliers — presumably Ledger among them — were “previously notified of the corporate acquisition and new management structure.”

Several people Zero Day spoke with say the months-long silence around the acquisition is "very shady" and question whether this was intended to keep Ledger customers in the dark while the implants spread through online sales. But Prabu says the suspicion, at least against them, is misplaced.

Oddly, Prabu did not identify who acquired CryptoBilis. He wrote that anyone who has questions about Ledger devices sold by CryptoBilis should contact Nicholas Chang. Chang, however, is identified in old postings to Facebook and X as a director of marketing for CryptoBilis, not the owner. Chang did not respond to an inquiry from Zero Day.

There is currently no evidence that anyone associated with CryptoBilis is behind the implants or the heist of cryptocurrency last week.

But the security researcher in Japan who has participated in conversations about the implants with Grand and Ledger since the spring, told Zero Day that he uncovered some intriguing findings from data he extracted from Ledger implants he purchased.

The researcher, who doesn't want to be publicly identified, purchased several Nano X wallets last March for his own use and put them in a drawer, intending to analyze them at some point when he had free time. After seeing Grand post his Tropicon slides online last spring, he took apart his own Ledger devices and found implants in them. He ended up purchasing ten Nano X devices from unauthorized Ledger sellers, most of them through the Amazon marketplace in Japan. One of the devices shipped from Malaysia, several came from Thailand, and two of them were shipped to him from an address in Osaka – essentially a shipping hub. All of them had implants. He found five different versions of implants among them, including the sophisticated implants Karpelès had found, as well as two additional designs.

"Some were very advanced and some were very basic," he says. "When I say versions [I mean] some of the layouts or components are different."

All of the implants operate in similar ways to record the randomly generated seed phrase as it's sent to the compromised device's screen and transmit the data to the attackers. He says he can't tell if the same group is behind all of the designs or if different actors took inspiration from an original design created by one person and advanced it.

In the case of the devices he received from Osaka, the seller's address was listed as a house in another city in Japan. That house, the researcher says, is used as an address for numerous companies engaged in various businesses, including criminal enterprises.

More interesting, he says, is that he was able to trace the transmission of the stolen seed data to servers in Hong Kong. The eSIM the attackers planted in Ledger devices is designed to work in any country, and the researcher says that if a device owner doesn't initialize their new wallet, the eSIM still retains the location of the last cell tower it connected to, which he was able to extract from the eSIMs in his wallets.

"This allowed me to find [what I think are] some manufacturing hubs for the implant," he says.

He says additional data contained in the compromised device's microcontroller firmware can be used to trace the location of the command and control servers used to receive the stolen seed phrase. He says he was able to trace the transmissions to servers hosted at a data center in Hong Kong that is managed by Alibaba and determined that in June at least 90 implants on infected Ledger devices were sending seed phrases to those servers, though he thinks the true number of devices communicating with the servers is likely much higher than this.

Pivot to Ledger Flex and Stax Devices

Although most of the compromised Ledger devices so far have been Nano X devices, there is evidence that the attackers have begun to pivot to Ledger Flex and Stax devices. Over the weekend someone posted images of their Stax device on X, which also appears to be compromised. It's not clear if this has been independently confirmed by Ledger or researchers. Separate to this, the researcher in Japan says he purchased two Ledger Flex devices and found implants in them as well.

He says that sometime in July or August he was monitoring a number of online sites that were selling Nano X devices when several of them stopped selling Nano X devices and switched to selling Ledger Flex devices.

"My sense is that they simply developed a new implant that is only for Flex," he says.

He says he has spoken with Japanese law enforcement about his findings as well as with technical contacts at Ledger, but the latter has not shared any information with him about its own investigation.

In the meantime, the list of compromised devices is growing. Over the weekend, Karpelès has been posting information from other Ledger device owners who have since found implants in their devices.

Update 12:30pm EST: SatoshiLabs, the Czech company that makes the Trezor wallets that compete with Ledger products, just announced that in light of implants found in Ledger devices sold by authorized sellers, SatoshiLabs is dramatically reducing its own list of approved sellers. Danny Sanders chief commercial officer for Trezor, wrote on X that the move is a "preventive step" and "there is not a single piece of evidence that Trezor devices have been compromised." In a letter Trezor sent to sellers who will be losing their authorization, Trezor wrote that they continue to sell devices they already have in stock but they will receive no new inventory, and as of January 1, 2027 Trezor will remove them from its list of authorized sellers.

item.title: Amazon pushes up prices across the Internet (608 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.not-ship.com/how-amazon-pushes-up-prices-all-across-the-internet/, See on Hacker News

Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition.

But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...

💙 Amanda

Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over: the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.

In a nutshell, here's what's happening:

This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.

Let's get into it.

Amazon charges sellers a lot of fees

Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales. But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!

Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.

Where an Amazon sale goes

Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising.

There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article.

Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice.

Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options:

In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising.

So, sellers have to raise prices

Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices.

Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too.

And they can't charge less elsewhere

Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller, if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales.

The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon.

It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit, California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target.

Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go.

There's no easy way out

For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales. For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option.

At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final.

After last week's piece, a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway.

FULL DISCLOSURE

I spent two years working at the Washington Post, which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos owns. During that time, he was busy dismantling the publication, so he wasn't well loved in the newsroom.

CLASSIC ENSHITTIFICATION

In August, I saw Cory Doctorow speak at the Edinburgh International Book Festival. His enshittification concept — the process by which online platforms shift from serving their users to squeezing them — inspired this two-part series on Amazon. If you want to understand it all a lot better, I highly recommend his book Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It. Somehow it makes antitrust issues both accessible and entertaining!

FROM ELSEWHERE

Here's what I found interesting, important or delightful this week:

Life after death? Alvin Chang's latest masterpiece has dropped! It’s about what people around the world believe happens after we die, drawn from surveys of nearly 130,000 people in 23 countries. (Proud to count Alvin as a Not-Ship subscriber 💙.)

Stunning embroidery. If you haven't seen the work of Irene Saputra, get yourself over to Instagram. Endlessly inspirational.

Instant knowledge. The Ars Notoria was a medieval magic book that promised scholars university learning through prayers, rituals and diagrams. No studying required!

item.title: Starlink limit hits Ukraine's drones. The battlefield depends on SpaceX (127 pts)

  • WIADOMOŚCI
  • ANALIZA

SpaceX has introduced a speed restriction affecting StarShield terminals used by Ukraine. According to Ukrainian sources, connectivity began to fail when platforms exceeded around 160 km/h, disrupting part of Ukraine’s combat missions. Later reports claimed that the restriction may have been tightened further, with some operators losing communication already at 60–70 km/h. If confirmed, that would no longer affect only fast strike drones, but also a much wider group of reconnaissance and tactical UAVs.

The first point is technical, but crucial. This is not a general shutdown of Starlink for the Ukrainian military. The issue concerns terminals used in motion, especially under the StarShield military package. The initial figure of around 160 km/h is important because it affects faster unmanned platforms, including strike systems and drones operating beyond classic radio-control range. A lower threshold of 60–70 km/h would be far more serious, because many ordinary tactical UAVs operate in that speed bracket.

It is also wrong to describe Starlink mainly as a navigation system for drones. Its real role is communication: command link, video transmission, mission updates and contact between operator and platform beyond direct line of sight. A drone may still know where it is going through GNSS, inertial systems or autonomous navigation, but without a reliable data link, it loses flexibility, live control and battlefield value. In drone warfare, the link is often as important as the airframe.

The political link is possible, not proven

Serhii Sternenko suggested that SpaceX’s decision could be connected to pressure from the Trump administration on Kyiv. Similar interpretations appeared in Ukrainian discussions, especially because the restriction comes amid tensions over Ukrainian strikes against targets in Russia. But this should not be presented as an established fact. SpaceX has not publicly confirmed such a motive. The White House has not confirmed that it ordered the change. Reuters has not established that the restriction came from the US administration.

The political context is obvious, but attribution is not the same as suspicion. What is already clear is that SpaceX can remotely change the operational parameters of terminals used on the battlefield. Even a narrow technical change, such as a speed limit, can immediately affect strike missions, reconnaissance and command links. For Ukraine, this is not only a question of one service update. It is a question of dependence.

A battlefield advantage and a strategic vulnerability

Earlier this year, mechanisms for verifying and limiting Starlink terminals helped Ukraine counter Russian use of the system on drones. The same kind of technical control now appears to have affected Ukrainian military users. This shows both the strength and the weakness of the system. Starlink and StarShield give Ukraine resilient communications that are difficult to replace. At the same time, Ukraine does not fully control the conditions under which that communications architecture operates.

That is the real military issue. The war in Ukraine has shown that private satellite networks can become part of the battlefield. But private infrastructure also means private control, contractual limits, geofencing, service parameters and political exposure. A state can build drones, train operators and plan missions, but if the data link depends on one external provider, the whole system remains vulnerable to decisions made outside the chain of command.

If the 60–70 km/h reports were confirmed, the consequences would go beyond fast strike drones. They would affect a larger part of Ukraine’s unmanned architecture and force operators to adapt missions, platforms and communications methods. The problem is therefore not simply that Starlink has imposed a speed limit. The problem is that one technical decision by SpaceX can change the tempo of Ukrainian drone operations almost immediately.

AMONG the many valuable contributions of William Dwight Whitney to linguistic science is one especially important and fundamental principle. It may be stated in these words. In explaining the prehistoric phenomena of language we must assume no other factors than those which we are able to observe and estimate in the historical period of language development. The factors that produced changes in human speech five thousand or ten thousand years ago cannot have been essentially different from those which are now operating to transform living languages. On the basis of this principle we look to-day at a much-discussed problem of Indo-European philology with views very different from the views held by the founders of Comparative Philology and their immediate successors. I refer to the problem, how the Indo-European people came to assign gender to nouns, to distinguish between masculine, feminine, and neuter. This question is of interest to others besides philologists. What man of culture who has learned languages such as the Greek, Latin, or French has not at times wondered that objects which have no possible connection with the natural gender of animals appear constantly in the language as male or female? In German, for example, it is der fuss, but die hand; der geist, but die seele; in Latin, hīc hortus, hīc animus, hīc amor, but haec planta, haec anima, haec felicitas; in Greek, ὁ πλοῦτος, ὁ οἶκος, but ἡ πενία, ἡ οἰκία.
This gender distinction pervades all the older Indo-European languages, and must therefore be regarded as having its origin in the time of the pro-ethnic Indo-European community. Not only is the subject itself full of interest, but also the treatment it has received from the philological research of our century. The various efforts made to solve the problem may very aptly illustrate an essential difference which exists between the theories of language development held in the beginning and middle of this century and those which prevail to-day, — a difference of method existing not in comparative linguistics alone, but also in other fields of philological and historical research that border on it.

item.title: AOSP Source Releases Are So Late Developers Disassemble Libraries to Report Bugs (463 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/android/ndk/issues/2260, See on Hacker News

Description

On Android 17 builds from September 2026, wcscspn() and wcspbrk() stop at the first character of the string that is >= U+0100 whenever the reject set has two or more characters that are all < U+0100. The character is reported as a match even though it is not in the set. wcsspn(), wcschr(), wcsrchr(), wmemchr() and wcsstr() are correct.

Any code that scans wide strings for ASCII delimiters, for example newline or wildcard characters, breaks as soon as the text contains an emoji, CJK, Cyrillic, Greek or Latin Extended character.

Affected / unaffected

Device Build Result
Pixel 7 google/panther/panther:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys broken
Pixel 8a google/akita/akita:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys (patch 2026-09-05) broken
Nothing Phone 2 Nothing/PongEEA/Pong:16/BQ2A.250721.001-BP2A.250605.031.A3 (patch 2026-08-01) ok

The public android17-release sources (android-17.0.0_r1, June 2026) build wcscspn/wcspbrk from external/llvm-libc, which is a plain nested loop over wchar_t and is correct. The code on the September builds is different (see "Mechanism"), so the regression was introduced between the June and September releases.

Reproducer

Build with the NDK (aarch64-linux-android30-clang), push to /data/local/tmp, run with adb shell:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <wchar.h>

int main(void)
{
    wchar_t s[] = {'a', 0x1F680, 0x100, 'b', 'x', '\n', 0};
    printf("wcscspn(s, L\"x\\n\") = %zu (expected 4)\n", wcscspn(s, L"x\n"));
    printf("wcspbrk(s, L\"x\\n\") = index %ld (expected 4)\n", (long)(wcspbrk(s, L"x\n") - s));
    printf("wcsspn(s, L\"a\\U0001F680\") = %zu (expected 2)\n", wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680"));
    return 0;
}

Output on CP3A.260905.009:

wcscspn(s, L"x\n") = 1 (expected 4)
wcspbrk(s, L"x\n") = index 1 (expected 4)
wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680") = 2 (expected 2)

A sweep of every code point from U+0001 to U+10FFFF (skipping surrogates and the two set members) with wcscspn(L"<cp>\n", L"x\n") returns 0 instead of 1 for 1,111,808 code points: every one from U+0100 to U+10FFFF. U+0001 to U+00FF are correct.

Which set shapes trigger it (all measured on the Pixel 8a):

Reject set Result
one character ok
two or more characters, all < U+0100 (e.g. L"x\n", L"\xe9\n") broken
two or more characters, at least one >= U+0100 ok
haystack limited to U+0080..U+00FF ok

Mechanism (from the shipped libc.so)

Disassembly of wcscspn in /apex/com.android.runtime/lib64/bionic/libc.so on CP3A.260905.009 shows three paths selected by the set:

  1. One character: a plain compare loop. Correct.
  2. Two or more characters: a 256-byte bool table on the stack is filled from the set while the set characters are in 1..0xFF. If a set character >= 0x100 is seen, the function falls back to calling wcschr() for each haystack character. Correct.
  3. Otherwise the haystack is scanned against the table:
a2564:  ldrb  w8, [x9, x8]        ; table[c]
a2568:  tbnz  w8, #0, a2578       ; in set -> stop (correct)
a256c:  ldr   w8, [x22, #0x4]!    ; next character
a2570:  cmp   w8, #0x100
a2574:  b.lo  a2564               ; c < 0x100 -> keep scanning
a2578:  ...                       ; c >= 0x100 -> STOP, reported as a match

A character >= 0x100 cannot be in a set whose members are all < 0x100, so for wcscspn the scan must continue past it. The code stops instead. wcsspn has the same structure, and there stopping is the correct answer (the character is not in the keep set), which is why only the complement functions are wrong. wcspbrk is implemented on top of this scan and inherits the bug.

The existing bionic test TEST(wchar, wcspbrk) in tests/wchar_test.cpp only uses ASCII input, so it does not catch this. A test such as EXPECT_EQ(3u, wcscspn(L"aĀb\n", L"x\n")) would.

Real-world impact

Visual Pinball on Android (libwinevbs, a Unix build of Wine's vbscript engine) stopped loading any table whose VBScript source contains a comment with an emoji after the September update: the lexer uses wcspbrk(ptr, L"\n\r") to skip comments, got the position of the first emoji instead of the line end, and reported "Invalid character". FileSystem.MoveFolder likewise treated every path containing a character >= U+0100 as a wildcard pattern via wcspbrk(src, L"*?><").

Worked around downstream by replacing the calls with plain loops: vpinball/libwinevbs#41 (shipped in vpinball/vpinball@e7837322f4).

Full disassembly of the affected functions and the probe sources are available on request.

I am using a supported NDK

It is with deep regret that we are announcing the cancellation of this year’s Grace Hopper Celebration in Anaheim, CA.

This is not a decision we made lightly; we understand it leaves many of our community disappointed. It is a function of not having the funds required to move forward with the Celebration, unlike in years past. Unlike past events, this year, both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations and, ultimately, below the level needed to cover critical operating expenses.

We know this decision affects far more than an event. Many of you have made travel arrangements, booked hotels, received visas, secured time away from work, organized teams, and planned important moments around being together. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this creates.

If you have plans to attend GHC, please take the following steps now:

  • Cancel or modify your airline, train, or other travel reservations directly with your travel provider.
  • Cancel hotel reservations made independently directly with the hotel or booking provider, and any other reservations or commitments connected to your trip.
  • Information regarding GHC registration, sponsorships, exhibitor commitments, and other financial matters will be communicated directly to the individuals and organizations affected. GHC has always been about more than a place or a moment on the calendar. It is about a community that has spent decades opening doors, expanding opportunity, and making sure women technologists have a voice in shaping the future of technology.

item.description:
URL: https://www.cphiri.dev/presentations/recreational-programming, See on Hacker News

Recreational Programming

You guys are getting paid?

Show of hands:

How many of you learned programming because it was fun?

Part 1

What is Recreational Programming?

Definition

Programming for the joy of programming itself - not for work, not for money, not for external requirements.

What it looks like:

  • Building things because you're curious how they work
  • Exploring new languages just to see what they feel like
  • Solving problems that only exist in your head
  • Creating tools for problems you don't actually have
  • Writing code that makes you smile

What it's NOT:

  • Side hustles or potential startups
  • Skill building for career advancement
  • Following tutorials step-by-step
  • Grinding through coding challenges for interviews
  • Building what others expect you to build

The key distinction: Internal motivation vs. external pressure

Why it matters:

  • Prevents burnout by reconnecting with intrinsic motivation
  • Develops intuition through low-stakes exploration
  • Maintains long-term passion for the craft
  • Often leads to unexpected breakthroughs and learning

Part 2

The Recreational Programming Spectrum

Style 1: The Live Explorer

  • Builds in public through streams or blogs
  • Shows the messy process: dead ends, bugs, restarts
  • Community becomes accountability and energy source
  • Projects range from practical tools to pure experiments

Style 2: The Deep Diver

  • Obsesses over understanding how things really work
  • Builds toy versions of complex systems
  • Values learning over shipping
  • Often has multiple "educational" implementations

Style 3: The Creative Technologist

  • Uses code as artistic medium
  • Generative art, music synthesis, interactive installations
  • Technology serves creative vision
  • Often blends programming with other disciplines

Style 4: The Problem Solver

  • Scratches personal itches with code
  • Tools that solve tiny annoying problems
  • "Good enough" solutions that work for them
  • Often accidentally builds useful things

Style 5: The Language Explorer

  • Constantly trying new languages and paradigms
  • Implements same concepts across different languages
  • Drawn to unusual or experimental languages
  • Code as intellectual curiosity

Part 3

Common Patterns Across All Styles

Permission to Build "Useless" Things

  • No business case required
  • Curiosity is sufficient justification
  • Failed experiments still teach valuable lessons

Key insight: ROI doesn't apply to recreational programming

Follow Energy, Not Plans

  • Switch projects when excitement fades
  • Multiple abandoned repos are exploration, not failure
  • Boredom is data about what interests you

Key insight: Boredom is data, not defeat

Document the Journey

  • Share process, not just results
  • Teaching forces deeper understanding
  • Creates connection with others on similar paths

Key insight: Narrate your decisions

Embrace the Learning Process

  • Beginner's mind in new domains
  • Comfortable with not knowing
  • Process over product

Key insight: Progress over perfection

Part 4

Your Personal Programming Playground

The Environment

  • Dedicated "experiments" folder/repo
  • No production concerns: minimal setup, no CI/CD pressure
  • Quick project initialization scripts
  • Version control optional

Approaches You Can Try

  • Weekly Experiments (2-4 hours exploring one new thing)
  • Scratch-Built Challenges (Build toy versions of tools you use)
  • Itch-Scratching Projects (Solve your own annoying problems)
  • Teaching Projects (Build something while explaining it)
  • Cross-Language Challenges (Same problem, different languages)

The Mindset Shifts

  • "What if..." instead of "I should..."
  • Progress over perfection
  • Learning over shipping
  • Curiosity over productivity

Part 5

Real Examples in the Wild

Zikani Nyirenda - The Practical Experimenter

  • Creates random but useful tools: browser automation, file organizers, Git utilities
  • Experiments across Go, Rust, Python, Vue, and React
  • "What small problem can I solve today?" approach to coding
  • Perfect example of scratching personal itches through code

github.com/zikani03

Jeremiah Chienda - The Full-Stack Experimenter

  • Explores different architectural patterns and frameworks
  • Builds tools that solve real problems while learning new technologies
  • Shows how recreational programming can span the entire tech stack

github.com/liwoo

Tsoding Daily - The Live Explorer

  • Streams 4+ hours daily building random projects from scratch
  • Built his own text editors, programming languages, ray tracers
  • Shows complete process including failures and debugging
  • "Let's see what happens if..." approach to everything

ThePrimeagen - The High-Energy Problem Solver

  • Creates CLI tools and Neovim plugins for personal workflow optimization
  • Infectious enthusiasm for dev tools and performance
  • Reacts to and critiques other developers' code/approaches
  • Makes optimization and tooling feel like extreme sports

Casey Muratori - The Systems Deep Diver

  • Handmade Hero: Building a complete game from scratch on stream
  • Explains every single line of code and system design decision
  • No libraries, understanding everything from first principles
  • Demonstrates that you can build modern software without frameworks

Ben Eater - The Educational Builder

  • Builds computers on breadboards, explains every component
  • Creates video series on how CPUs, memory, and networks actually work
  • Takes months to build what you could buy for $5
  • Makes hardware fundamentals accessible and fascinating

Dan Luu - The Deep Technical Investigator

  • Writes detailed blog posts investigating performance mysteries
  • Benchmarks everything: keyboards, terminals, programming languages
  • Turns curiosity about "why is X slow?" into multi-thousand word research
  • Demonstrates how recreational investigation can uncover industry-wide issues

Each represents a different path back to programming joy

Closing Challenge

Pick one experiment:

  1. Build the worst possible version of a tool you use daily
  2. Spend 2 hours with a language you've been curious about
  3. Document yourself solving a small problem
  4. Fork an interesting project and mess with it
  5. Try live coding or streaming your process

The only rule: Stop if it stops being fun.

Final Thought

"The goal isn't to become any of these programmers. It's to remember why you started coding and keep that curiosity alive alongside your career."

An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody.

An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco.

Alfozan has worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors said.

OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted.

Surveillance footage shows Alfozan near the room on multiple dates before the discovery, though he was not authorized to enter the room or attend meetings there, prosecutors said. Meetings in the room frequently involved confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and government engagements, according to the complaint.

Before the device was installed, Alfozan used a productivity tool to ask about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities, and calendars, as well as the locations of leadership and outside partner meetings, the complaint alleges.

A chatbot account tied to Alfozan’s spouse, which shared identifiers with his own account, submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 about building, installing, obscuring, and remotely accessing a recording device, prosecutors said. Queries included how to “build a continuous audio recorder” and “encrypt the SD card,” prosecutors claimed. On Sept. 27 and 28, the account asked about the specific device that was later found, including its unique MAC address.

On Oct. 5, the complaint says, Alfozan entered the conference room and appeared to look behind the television. That same day, he allegedly left a bag unattended in a different room. Security personnel who opened it found his wallet and ID, along with a second recording device similar to the first.

“For us it is a matter of national security,” U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said in a statement.

FBI Director Kash Patel said protecting U.S. AI innovation is among the bureau’s highest counterintelligence priorities. Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI’s San Francisco field office, said the agency is committed to protecting sensitive research and proprietary technology.

If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release.

The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Northern District of California.

OpenAI said on X (opens in new tab) that after discovering the device, employees used the company’s AI models to determine what it was and where it came from, and referred the matter to the FBI. The company thanked the agents and prosecutors who “moved quickly to make an arrest.”

According to OpenAI, its technical surveillance countermeasures team found the device during a sweep of a conference room.

  • That flag-wrapped anti-AI bus in SF? A conservative group drove it here

  • Asking a chatbot about your ballot? Read this first

  • Trump wants to rebrand AI “Super intelligence.” Will Silicon Valley play along?

OpenAI described the device as sophisticated and designed to evade detection, saying it had advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data in a way meant to avoid monitoring. The company said investigators used its models to analyze forensic images of the device’s storage and assess changes in the underlying data.

The company said it has evidence that Alfozan intended to place other recording devices in sensitive spaces to secretly record meetings.

According to OpenAI, Alfozan was a member of the product team. The company said it coordinated the timing of his firing with the FBI to avoid disrupting the investigation, and he was terminated Friday, the day he was arrested. Between Sept. 30 and that date, OpenAI said, it gradually restricted his access to systems and spaces, then suspended his physical and network access, placed him on leave, and secured his company-issued equipment.

A YouTube video last month touted him as the only Saudi employee at OpenAI.

“Honestly, this one year felt like five years anywhere else,” he said in response to a question about his experience.

“The idea of AI is that it handles things one might not want to do, so they can focus on tasks or hobbies they enjoy more or work they take pleaseure in and let it do the tedious tasks,” Alfozan said later in the video.

A LinkedIn profile that matches Alfozan’s name lists his OpenAI role as engineering lead on the company’s AI agents platform

Before joining OpenAI, he was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI infrastructure company for logistics, from 2022 to August 2025, according to the LinkedIn profile. From 2017 to 2022, he was a senior systems engineer at Meta. His earlier experience, according to the profile, includes a stint as a systems engineer at Reach Labs, a wireless power startup in Y Combinator’s summer 2015 batch, and internships at Microsoft, SAP in Berlin and Akamai Technologies.

He has a master’s degree in data science from UC Berkeley, the LinkedIn profile says.

A man in the passenger seat of a car at Alfozan’s Millbrae home said that the family did not want to speak to reporters.

OpenAI said it has no indication that Alfozan improperly accessed or took model weights, source code, or customer data and has not seen activity that compromised the safety of its products or customers’ information. The company said it will continue to support the FBI’s investigation.

OpenAI said it treats protecting its technology, data and people “as a matter of national importance” and called the case an example of how AI can counter sophisticated security threats.

A detention hearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse is set for Oct. 19.
